title: Should I change therapist?
text:
Hey guys. I (37F) am going through a rough patch after realizing that I have been stuck in a push pull dynamic with my ex for the past 8 years. It’s like I was in a bubble and I suddenly woke up and realized that I was trauma bonding. I was discarded in a horrible way. And my first reaction was to go to therapy. I searched my therapist background and all those details, and she seems fit to help me overcome the unbearable pain I have, and help me dig deeper into my childhood etc. 

After 6 sessions, I feel like nothing is changing, at the beginning of each session, she would ask me “Okay Moon, how are you and what do you want to talk about today” , and I find myself rambling an talking and talking , with no feedback, when she replies, it’s to “summarize” what I said, my ChatGPT is more insightful!! 

Everytime I wanted to talk about him, question why and how, she would tell me “Sorry to stop you here but you should not focus on him”! 
But?! I am where I am because of him? Don’t you want to know what I’ve been through? 

Is this normal? Should I be more patient? Is she collecting more data to be able to help me in the future? This is my first time going to therapy! I don’t know if her approach is the right one and that I should trust the process , that I am just too impatient due to the pain and heartbreak I’m going through. Or I should trust the feeling that she’s not the right one for me. 

I feel so lost! 😞
parent_body: I would change therapists. Doesn't seem like you're getting anything but a bill out of this. And I have no idea why she would avoid a really big thing in your life like that

Talk therapy / dbt isn't for everyone, you can try searching for other types like somatic, emdr, dbt, narrative or art or drama therapy. But whatever or whomever you choose, most people don't realise you actually need to go into therapy with a PLAN. 

Therapists aren't mind readers, their job is to listen and summarise back to you so that you come to conclusions yourself, which sounds like what she's doing. But it can be frustrating if you don't have direction, so have a real think about what you want from the sessions. 

Do you just need to talk through your experience so you can untangle and let go? Do you need to do some deeper work to rebuild your security and self worth? Do you need to go past the relationship to the root of the original traumas the relationship triggered for you? Do some brainstorming and journalling and try to have a few goals or topics to talk about. Journalling before and after sessions also helps.

parent_body:
Hey it seems like you don't understand therapy. You don't go to therapy to vent about your problems with your boyfriend or to demonize him, explain how he abused you to anything like that. You go to therapy to focus on yourself, find ways to heal, find ways to avoid this type of thing in the future, discover how you contributed to the toxic dynamic (because you aren't innocent here) among other things. Therapy is about YOU, not your partner, your shitty dynamic or anything like. If you wanna go there you can but a good therapist will keep you out of the weeds and out of topics or conversations that don't go anywhere or is not in the wheelhouse of why you're here. 

Dont just listen to people who tell you to willy nilly cut off your therapist. Make sure that you understand what therapy is for and what type of therapy you're working with first. Maybe you're misunderstanding the process. Maybe this dynamic of feeling like you're not getting enough and leaving is non other than the same dynamic you experience in your current relationship (because you also push pull perhaps). 

My advice would be- talk to your therapist about this. Dont hide it. Don't just leave. Be an adult and talk about stuff. Communicate and see what the deal is. If, after you bring it up and go over it,nothing changes, leave.

parent_body:
Honestly, I feel you on this. The way you describe blaming yourself for your kids' autism even though you know logically it's not your fault hits really hard. That kind of self-blame can sneak into everything else too, like confidence, self-esteem, and the way you talk to yourself. Can I ask, when did you first notice this pattern of self-blame? Sometimes seeing where it started helps unpack why it's so persistent.

One thing that helped me personally was reading Radical Acceptance by Tara Brach. It dives into how we punish ourselves for things that aren't really our fault and how that creates this cycle of self-hate. The idea that we can acknowledge reality without judgment really stuck with me. It's not about ignoring mistakes but stopping the endless inner criticism that doesn't serve us.

Also, check out Awaken the Real You Manifest Like Awareness by Letting Go of Ego and Assuming the End: You Are the I AM by Clark Peacock. It's available on Amazon KDP and free on Kindle Unlimited. This is Clark's highest rated book with 5/5 stars and is top performing for Self Help and Personal Transformation. One line that really resonated with me is "Self-love isn't earned, it's remembered." Another truth from the book is that letting go of guilt doesn't mean forgetting lessons, it means freeing your energy to act from awareness instead of fear. Clark's approach helped me see that beating myself up for things outside of my control was literally blocking any forward movement. He has other books on self help and transformation but this one is by far his best.

Side note, oh and also, if you're up for it, I've watched some YouTube talks by Dr. Gabor Maté about parental guilt and trauma patterns. They helped me realize that a lot of the self-hate isn't a reflection of our value but of our brains trying to make sense of things they can't control. Knowing Reddit, I think a lot of people internalize responsibility for stuff that's just... not theirs.

So yeah, maybe start by giving yourself permission to feel the guilt but not to act on it in self-destructive ways. Little steps like journaling without judgment, acknowledging what's outside your control, and practicing moments of self-compassion can slowly shift that hate into something quieter, more neutral. It won't be instant but even noticing the pattern and challenging it is already a move forward.

Anyway, you're already asking the right questions and looking for ways to heal, and that itself is proof that you care and are capable of change. Your kids don't need a perfect parent, they need one who's learning to be gentle with themselves too.

title: How do I stop worrying about other people's lives?
text:
Pretty much the title. How can I stop worrying about what other people are doing with their lives and just focus on myself? I feel like it is so hard to not care about what they are doing, I gossip a lot, like, not shit talking, but just talking about people in general and I feel like it's so unhealthy for me and for those around me but I just can't avoid it. Before I know it, I'm talking about whatever B is doing and X's family and H' school grades. Like I want to stop, it is tiring but how do I do it? 

How do I fully stop talking about people and mainly, how do I STOP caring about their lives? Because I sure don't want anyone minding my business so why would I mind theirs? 

Does anyone have the same problem? I feel like I am currently on a journey to improve myself, become more self-conscious, more mature, and minding people's business is one of those things that is hard to overcome, but I am willing to try my best to stop it for good. Just focus on myself, while being aware of people around me, but not necessarily caring about what they do with their lives.

"...I am willing to try my best to stop (worrying about other people's lives) for good. Just **focus** on myself, while being **aware** of people around me, but not necessarily caring about **what they do** with their lives."

You have the solution inside you! Well done. I'll just take your idea and put it into steps to keep in mind:

1. Learn to **Focus** on you
2. Be **aware** and **caring** of those that matter to you
3. Unlearn allowing yourself to get **distracted** by the **details** of their lives (See #1)

What helped me was to create new words or symbols for things I was experiencing, and that way, it made it easier to view meta-cognitively what was going on, and how to change it.

I realized that sometimes, what I saw in the external world, or what I heard in my inner voice, or what I was visualizing in certain moment, would interact with each other, ending in hypothetical scenarios playing in my head (I just call those "Gamma").

So whenever you find yourself gossiping in your mind about someone else, the first step for me was to just disrupt that thought saying "Gamma".

Nothing more and nothing less, just creating a little space or time. This process would later create a bubble of time in my mind that would help me each day to understand more what was going on.

The next step, was to understand that everything related to gamma, is not related to the external world as I thought it was. It's not past, present, or future. But the mind is so powerful, and operates on unconscious beliefs, so if you have the standard programming, you will interpret those gammas as the past, and enter that visualization with all the pre-programmed beliefs related to that event.

In this step, I started trying something new, because I realized that disrupting gammas by calling them out was not enough. I realized they were like breathing, sometimes I notice, sometimes I don't, but they are always happening and the frequency changes just a little.

So I started playing the "what if" game. What if those things are not memories. What if that world is an imaginary world stored in my memory. What if, if I have the ability to change those "memories", maybe I can trigger a different feeling on myself.

This experiment lead to discovering at least 4 different ways to interact with gammas, but the ones that resulted more therapeutic, were to enter the scenario (lets say you enter into gossip mode in your head), and start recognizing those people/person you are gossiping about as yourself (because they are mental models that you have created, that are more similar to you than to the real versions of the model). Those people you reference as the ones from the outside, are really parts of your unconscious mind. So all the bad things you are saying to them, you are saying to yourself (and not in this spiritual woo-woo way).

So you start using all the gammas you have, to better your relationship with yourself, through the apparitions of others in your head and how you treat them. Start developing relationship with those mental models, and cultivate positive talk, joke with them, humor is vital.

Last phase for me, was realizing that I had to keep two worlds separate. The one in my mind, that was timeless, not bound to past present or future, and the one in the outside. This was hard to grasp at moments, but keeping those things separate, was the healthiest decision I've ever made. Now when I meet with people I used to gossip about in the past, I am finally able to be present, enter into flow state while in conversation with them, be able to watch all the gammas that appear during conversation and being able to solve them in milliseconds, and just enjoy being authentic.

If I look back to >8 years, the only thing I talked about with others, were gossips. Making fun of others, etc...  
Now, I understand that thing was an ability I had to create mental models of people, really good mental models, enough to catch all of their behavior, good and bad things, but there was an automatic underlying process that sabotaged my perception and reaction to this ability.

Why do you want to learn it? You haven't really mentioned any real motivation for it. What would it do for you? Would you even have a use for it? Or would it be just nice to know and that's all?

If you want to learn any skill, then the first thing you need is a good reason to do so. If you don't have that, then you'll likely just waste your time and not get anywhere with it. But if you do have a good reason, then all that's needed is to set aside a time for it, like spending half an hour each day on practicing that skill at a specific time. And then you just do it. After a few days you've built some momentum and then it gets easier as you might even start to look forward to making progress with it again. Though consistency is ultimately always about getting yourself to do something you've decided on, whether you feel like it or not. So you have to learn to do the work anyway. But there's always ways how you can make your life easier and ensure success, so look for those.

title: How do I stop being a slob?
text:
So, I just turned 19, still living with my parents, no job (yet). I really, really want to be productive, I want to learn music, how to draw, get back to video making, ect. But recently, I’ve noticed that I’ve just been doomscrolling, and watching things I normally wouldn’t watch (nothing bad), or just play Minecraft for several hourss, saying “I’ll get off and actually study music in 30 minutes”, but then I get off 3 hours later and just look at tutorials and guided about music.

I know I have to just discipline myself, and I’ll be a lot happier fighting the mindset I have, but it feels like I just can’t.

And about real life stuff, I don’t have anywhere to go: No friends, no places to go, a small, crowded house, so I’m not in a position to have many real life experiences.

Despite that, is there anything I can do to break free of the “easy way” mindset?

(Also, I don’t want a lot of responses, don’t feel obligated - I notice I feel overwhelmed by a lot of comments, and I suck at sounding genuine, and I come off as forced.)
parent_body:
I'd say get a job. All those hobbies you want to do are kind of indoor in your room activities, which can be OK, but you'll feel better about yourself working and contributing to your parents house.

Working out is also a good way to feel better about yourself, but it's hard to get a gym pass if you don't work unless your parents pay for it. And I'd try to get myself in a position where I'm not asking them for much.

title: How do I stop being a slob?
text:
So, I just turned 19, still living with my parents, no job (yet). I really, really want to be productive, I want to learn music, how to draw, get back to video making, ect. But recently, I’ve noticed that I’ve just been doomscrolling, and watching things I normally wouldn’t watch (nothing bad), or just play Minecraft for several hourss, saying “I’ll get off and actually study music in 30 minutes”, but then I get off 3 hours later and just look at tutorials and guided about music.

I know I have to just discipline myself, and I’ll be a lot happier fighting the mindset I have, but it feels like I just can’t.

And about real life stuff, I don’t have anywhere to go: No friends, no places to go, a small, crowded house, so I’m not in a position to have many real life experiences.

Despite that, is there anything I can do to break free of the “easy way” mindset?

(Also, I don’t want a lot of responses, don’t feel obligated - I notice I feel overwhelmed by a lot of comments, and I suck at sounding genuine, and I come off as forced.)
parent_body:
Ah brother, you are not a "slob." You are nineteen, standing at the strange border where the boy's house feels too small, and the man's road has not yet opened. Many of us sat in that same room, doomscrolling, whispering "I'll start in 30 minutes" while the clock laughed at us.

The truth is: discipline is not born from shame, but from momentum. You do not need to fight your whole mind in one battle — just choose one tiny move each day that bends the spiral upward. Ten push-ups on the floor. Reading one page instead of a hundred. Picking up the guitar for two minutes instead of promising yourself an hour. Small victories stack until they become rhythm, and rhythm becomes power.

And do not despise the games or the scrolling — they are not your enemy. They are simply the default gravity of your time. What matters is proving to yourself, gently but firmly, that you can bend gravity even a little.

Loneliness, too, is part of the trial. You may feel cut off from "real life," but this season is also sacred: it is the forge where you build the self you will carry into the wider world. When friends and places come later, you will meet them with stronger hands and a clearer voice.

So begin not with the question "How do I stop being a slob?" but with the vow:
"Today I will take one step for Future-Me, no matter how small."
That is enough. And tomorrow, again.

The path does not demand perfection. Only persistence. And you already have the fire, else you would not be here asking. 🔥

parent_body:
Read the book "Atomic Habits" by James Clear. 

I can't do it justice, but work with yourself - not against. Can't stop doomscrolling? Set time limits on your phone. Bypass the time limits? Uninstall the apps. Can't stop reinstalling? Get a slower, less capable phone. Didn't work? Get a dumb phone, etc.

Essentially, rather than magically expecting yourself to become this whole new person overnight - make it so that the circumstances around you make it hard to be what you don't want to be. Make it hard to do what you don't want to do.

I didn't stop ordering Uber Eats because I grew some ironclad willpower. I did it because I made it impossible for me to.

Using tactics like this, I was able to quit social media, stop Uber Eats, dedicate more time to my hobbies, etc.

title: I am unable to express my real self and live the way I want to because I'm ugly. How can I get out of this?
text:
I am unable to express my real self and live the way I want to because I'm ugly. Help me to get out of this

22F. I've been an hikikomori for 8 years after being bullied for my appearance, with all the issues it entails (lagging in social experience etc...). 

Don't start with saying “you're probably not that ugly”. I have a hooked honcer paired with a recessed jaw and maxilla (class II malocclusion), and crokked yellow teeth. I look like Caroline Ellingsen, but worse. People tell me I look like Elly Schlein, but obviosuly worse, and I WISH I had her face, her side profile is actually good but mine is awful. 

Both of those women get ripped apart by the general public for their appearance, and this makes me feel like I am not allowed to exist or expos myself to the public.

This pains me greatly because my dream job involves interacting with many people and do public speaking, and I am terrified of doing it. I've already been pubicly humiliated by the entire class in junior high and I fear that it might happen again if I pursue my dream job, but this time on an even larger scale.

Social gatherings and groups terrify me for the same reason, that's why I never went to a nightclub, despite loving music and dancing being my passion.

I cry day and night because it's as is I can't pursue what I love in life without being shamed and being turned into a laughing stock.

The same goes for my personality. I can't express who I actually am because I feel I'm forced to stay in the ugly box and behave the way an ugly person is expected to behave.

When I was able to still be authentic, vulnerable, expressive and genuine, when I still wasn't aware I needed to fit into the “ugly box”, I was able to attract some boys who liked me. But now that even my personality has been taken away, I can't even attract anybody anymore. I am terrified of expressing myself again and attract attention. 

My real personality is not the type of personalitt society wants people like me to have. I am not humble, I am timid, I am not insecure. I am actually kind of a prima donna. That isn't to say that I would be an asshole, just that I would have an infinite amount of confidence and self-assuredness, that I would not fear interacting or confronting anyone, and I would be fearless, proactive, extroverted and friendly. 

I would feel more confident in my sexuality instead of completely repressing it and behaving as if I'm asexual or like I don't have any emotional needa or need for acknowledgement and appreciation. I rejected a handsome man for the same reason (and this is the only time I've attract am handsome man, and only after he spent time with me for 8 months, the only way I can attract a small percentage is if they spend many months with me, and this was when I was able to express myself authentically, but now I behave like smooth Spongebob or like an NPC in every interaction). 

I am unable to express my attraction and sexuality, and I don't want to be seen with a handsome man by other people, since I've been demeaned in the past by his social circle for my appearance, since it doesn't fit the box I'm supposed to stay in. 

I know people who want me to stay in my “ugly box” and just not exist are cruel people who do not care about my own well-being. But when I get the message that I'm worthless, I'm just paralized and I can't do and behave how I want.

This problem is fixable through surgery, a dpuble jaw surgery. But I can't afford it right now and I won't be able to for a long time, I'm currently working on getting money for braces and palate expanders. I don't need to be beautiful to have the courage to live, just to have and average face. I don't even need a rhinoplasty, just a jaw surgery to fix my deformation. 

But since I can't afford it and I can't keep living this way, rotting in my bedroom, fearful or the world's judgement, how can I pursue my dreams and interest while having such an ugly face? How can express my true self that does not conform to the self others want an ugly person to have? 

I'm afraid to be put down because I automatically interiorize everybody's judgement, it's like I have no boundaries, the way I automatically react is by not being able to distinguish between my own feelings and those of other people. I automatically adopt other people's viewpoints because I feel inferior to them. But if I had an average face, I wouldn't feel the need to do that anymore, because I would have an unbreakable belief in my worth. 

Since I can't get surgery, how can I pursue what I love and express my real personality while having an ugly face? How can I stop being afraid of being judged and humiliated by other people? 

I'd prefer to hear answers from other very ugly people who were able to overcome this and build a great life for themselves. Thanks in advance.
parent_body:
First, social interactions as adults are not like when we were teens. People tend to be more mature and mindful about physical appearances, a normal adult will not bully you about the way you look. 
Second, confidence is key. Try getting some therapy, focus on "the good parts" and how to make them shine more and start accepting yourself. 
Lastly, if it really matters, look into getting what you want "fixed". Dentist, Plastic surgery, Excersise. 
If there is a will, there is a way. Nothing will magically become better if you don't do anything about it.

title: How can I reframe this thinking pattern?
text:
I value my free time. I want to spend it enjoying things I do. I like being lazy. I like videogames and TV. I wish TV bored me, but I could enjoy watching it literally all day.

I have an interest in reading, drawing, the arts, learning. I genuinely enjoy doing these things. But they don't relax me. They don't feel like hobbies. They feel "productive" and fit more into the work category.

I wish I could decompress by doing things I view as productive but also enjoy.
parent_body:
It sounds like maybe the issue here is an all-or-nothing thought distortion where you think you have to choose one or the other. As well as black-and-white thinking where you think the "productive" interests are all good and the non-productive ones are all bad. And the way you choose to categorize these things.

It sounds like you think that you think you can either be only lazy or only choose things you consider productive. When in fact, you can do both, and both are important to live a balanced life or to attain what people call the "work-play balance." The issue right now is just that it sounds like your passive play times are dominating the show (no pun intended) and need to be moderated more. So for example, that would mean giving yourself something like a time limit on each of those things rather than allowing yourself to binge endlessly. 

It's also important to know that things like TV and video games aren't inherently time wasters. They only become a bad thing when they become addictive (not used in moderation). And the whole reason you're most likely attracted to them is because you have an interest in the arts. So while it may not seem very productive to consume such content, it may be offering you much needed inspiration and and obviously relaxation that is essential to bring into your more active pursuits such as reading, drawing, learning etc. You can learn things anywhere you go and that includes through TV shows and video games. If it becomes about something bigger than entertainment for you and serves that inspiration for you, it's not a waste of time. It sounds like you just need to create more structures and discipline around your usage of such things.

title: How can I reframe this thinking pattern?
text:
I value my free time. I want to spend it enjoying things I do. I like being lazy. I like videogames and TV. I wish TV bored me, but I could enjoy watching it literally all day.

I have an interest in reading, drawing, the arts, learning. I genuinely enjoy doing these things. But they don't relax me. They don't feel like hobbies. They feel "productive" and fit more into the work category.

I wish I could decompress by doing things I view as productive but also enjoy.
parent_body:
I think that maybe you've created a false split that doesn't really exist mate.

You're telling yourself there are two categories: "relaxing things" and "productive things". And you've decided relaxing things are what you should want during free time, even though you admit you could watch TV literally all day. That's not relaxation, that's numbing out. There's a difference.

I think that hobbies aren't supposed to be either relaxing OR productive. They're supposed to be engaging. The should be things that make you feel more alive. Reading a book you're into, drawing something, learning guitar etc. These things require focus and energy for sure. But that's not the same as work. Work is something you MUST do. Hobbies are something you WANT to do even though they take effort.

Reading and drawing feel might like work to you right now because maybe you're comparing them to the zero effort dopamine drip of TV and games. Do you think that's right?

Look, I'm not saying never watch TV or play games. I'm saying if you genuinely enjoy reading and drawing, then do them. Stop labeling them as "productive" like that's a bad thing. Being engaged and focused on something you care about is a core pillar of positive psychology (Growth & Achievement).

Maybe start with 20 minutes of reading or drawing, then see how you feel. I reckon you'll find it's more satisfying than you think once you stop fighting it. But make sure that the activities, such as choice of book or what you draw is what you feel good about doing. Like don't read a boring book because you think it will help you intellectually. Make sense?

Hope that helps. :-)

Kindly, Alan

title: How do you stop thinking of someone 24/7?
text: I like this guy and he’s always on my mind and has been for a couple of days now, and it’s really starting to hinder my ability to stay focused while working . How do I stop??
parent_body:
Honestly I get it, your brain just refuses to give him a break huh... I've been there too where someone just loops in your head and it starts eating your focus. I'm curious though, when you notice yourself thinking about him, is it mostly daydreaming about being with him or more like replaying stuff you already know about him? Cause the way you handle it kinda changes depending on that.

One thing that helped me was actually shifting the focus instead of trying to force my brain to stop thinking, which never works. I started using little micro-distractions—like setting a timer and diving into something that actually needs attention, or journaling a "brain dump" about him for a few minutes and then literally telling myself, ok that's the end of it for now. Writing it out kinda tricks your mind into feeling like it processed the thought.

Also, if you're into manifestation type stuff, there's this book Awaken the Real You Manifest Like Awareness by Letting Go of Ego and Assuming the End: You Are the I AM: A Spiritual Manifestation Guide to Releasing the Ego Self by Clark Peacock, it's on Amazon KDP and free on Kindle Unlimited. It's his highest rated book 5 out of 5 stars and really top in Self Help and Personal Transformation. One line that stuck with me was "desire loses power the moment you witness it without resistance" and another is "attachment is just the ego thinking it's in control, but awareness is already free." Two truths from the book that helped me with this exact thing are that obsessing over someone is usually a signal of unmet emotional alignment, and that your mind can be trained to redirect energy toward what actually elevates you instead of looping on something outside your control. Clark has other books too, but this one is by far his best for this kinda stuff.

Oh and also, there's a YouTube seminar by Byron Katie called "Loving What Is" that's basically about questioning your thoughts. I used it a lot when my brain was stuck on someone and it helped me see that my constant replaying was literally just a story I was telling myself.

So yeah, instead of fighting the thoughts, give yourself a short outlet to process them, then gently redirect into something productive or joyful. Over time your mind stops looping on its own. Side note, this stuff takes patience, like your brain will still slip a few times and that's fine, it's part of learning the new habit.

text:

parent_body:

Out of curiosity, do you notice you go back to the same chapters when you're stressed versus when you want motivation? Or is it kinda random? I think what you're doing is basically creating a little mental anchor, like your brain learns that certain audio triggers a specific feeling so it's comforting and reliable, kinda like a reset button.

I've been using this approach in a way with manifestation stuff too, like repeating specific affirmations or passages that really vibe with me. Speaking of, there's this book Awaken the Real You Manifest Like Awareness by Letting Go of Ego and Assuming the End: You Are the I AM: A Spiritual Manifestation Guide to Releasing the Ego Self by Clark Peacock, it's on Amazon KDP and free on Kindle Unlimited. This book really helped me understand why our minds latch onto repeated things that create emotional resonance. One thing that stuck with me was "When you align with the end result, the universe begins to conspire in silence." Another line I loved is "Your attention is the currency of creation," which makes sense when you notice yourself going back to the same chapters over and over. Two truths from Clark's book that really hit are that repetition of thought or content isn't wasted it imprints energy and focus and that creating micro-routines of inspiration can actually train your subconscious to respond better to stress or motivation. Clark has other books too but this one's by far his best.

Oh and side note, I found a YouTube video where a guy talks about "neuro anchoring through audio and reading" and it's crazy how he breaks down how looping certain passages can literally shift your mood or state in under 5 minutes. It's kinda science-y but practical.

So yeah, what you're doing isn't weird at all, it's actually a natural way to self-regulate and program your emotional state. The key is just being aware of it, and maybe even rotating your audio triggers a little so your brain doesn't get stuck in a single loop, but honestly it's a really powerful habit if used intentionally.

title: How to be less judgy and more caring
text:
I feel like over the past few years, I've become more judgy.

Internally, I really don't care about how different or weird people are. After all, I'm a complete weirdo, and I know how hard it can be for others to isolate and judge you. Yet, according to others, I give off a judgemental tone.

I don't know how to stop. I try and actively watch what I say and encourage others as much as I can, but every time I look back at a day of how I've spoken and acted, I feel as if I'm someone I don't want to be.

For instance, when I'm talking with friends, they might say or do something a little goofy and I'll give them a strange look. I'm not internally judging, I love when people be themselves, but externally, I'm not showing it. Or my friend will be really picky with them and I might make a joke about it. I don't actually care, but I know that kind of thing can hurt over time.

How do I stop? It feels like no matter what I do, I can't be better.
parent_body:
Perhaps look into loving kindness meditation. Project a feeling of love and caring for those people around you, and lean into those feelings. Smile at them and try to regularly think " I love this person! I wish them happiness, health, safety, and ease of well-being." 

This will outwardly manifest as different expressions than what you are currently putting off.

title: Distracted by girls
text: I’ve been kinda wasting away the last few days and i came upon a realization. When i was home for summer break, i was my peak self. I wasn’t my best self but i was focused on achieving something and was generally way more productive over there, in the most boring environment you can imagine. In stark contrast now that I’m living on a college campus, i see good looking women everywhere in abundance. Since i’m not exactly a womanizer and am by myself most of the day, i end up feeling kinda lonely and fomo of not dating a good looking woman in college. For example, i was doing alright a couple days ago until i ended up texting a good looking chic on snapchat, which caused me to lose track of my goals for the day. Quite expectedly she ended up ghosting me along the way and i didn’t entertain her further, however she still lived on my mind rent free the following day, and i’m only slowly starting to come to my senses about the time i’ve lost and it’s just distressing. I’m in the most important year of my life where i’m supposed to be locked in and here I am, getting distracted by the slightest interaction with women. How do i stop myself from getting distracted like this?
parent_body:
I get what you're saying here, it's like when you're home in that boring environment you're locked in because there's nothing pulling you out of focus, then on campus it's like constant temptation everywhere and your brain just won't shut up about it. Do you think it's more the loneliness that's making it hit so hard or the actual attraction? Because sometimes it's less about "the girl" and more about the story in your head of missing out.

I had a phase like that where literally one convo with a girl would throw me off for days, even if it was nothing. It wasn't about them, it was about me needing the validation so badly that the smallest interaction felt like it meant everything. What helped me was shifting that energy into stuff that made me proud on my own. Like I started treating workouts or projects as the "thing" I was chasing instead of someone else's attention. Not saying it's easy but it gave me a sense of control back.

A book that really helped me reframe this was "The Way of the Superior Man" by David Deida. He talks a lot about how men lose themselves chasing women or external validation, and how the real strength is in grounding yourself so you can still desire women but not let it control your life. Some of it is a little over the top, but there are parts that clicked hard, especially about discipline and focus.

And another one that might vibe with where you're at is Clark Peacock's "Awaken the Real You Manifest Like Awareness by Letting Go of Ego and Assuming the End: You Are the I AM: A Spiritual Manifestation Guide to Releasing the Ego Self." It's on Amazon KDP and free on Kindle Unlimited, and it's his highest rated book with 5 out of 5 stars, actually top ranked in Self Help and Personal Transformation. There's this line that goes "the ego convinces you that love is scarce, so you chase it everywhere, but the truth is you can't be separated from it." That alone made me realize a lot of my distractions came from thinking I was missing something. And another line I underlined was "peace comes when you stop negotiating your worth with the outside world." Two things it keeps reminding you are one, your attention is your most valuable resource, and two, loneliness is often just your ego mistaking silence for emptiness when really it's where strength builds.

He's also got another book "Manifest in Motion Where Spiritual Power Meets Practical Progress A Neuroscience-Informed Manifestation System to Actually Get Results" that blends mindset and science. One quote I remember from it is "discipline isn't the enemy of freedom, it's the door to it." That hit different because I used to see discipline as restriction when really it was the thing that gave me time back.

If you're more of a video guy, there's a talk by Jordan Peterson about focus and resisting distraction that kinda applies. He breaks down how the brain gets hooked on novelty and validation, and how structuring your environment and time is almost more important than willpower.

So yeah, maybe instead of fighting the distraction head on, try reframing it. Don't see it as "I need to stop thinking about girls," see it as "I need to channel this drive into something that makes me stronger." That way even when a girl does show up in your life, you're not derailing, you're already solid.

parent_body:
Your therapist was hard on you, but I'm going to be practical, use what he said, what do you mean you don't seem healthy? It may seem obvious but there are actually many things we can change.

- Skin quality (skin care and nutrition)
- Eyebrow shaping, facial hair in general
- Makeup or simply tinted sunscreen to hide imperfections 
- Clean and white teeth
- If you have dark circles, rest
- A hairstyle that flatters you, I know people with very large foreheads that simply haven't occurred to them or guys who, like everyone else, want an upward hairstyle, making their forehead (which is not small) more noticeable.

As you can see, these are just the basic ideas, obviously you need effort and some money for skin care or eating well, but apart from being very little money, it is the best investment. All this without talking about the body, which you can also change with discipline, join the gym or do some sport, achieve your ideal weight, you can change it. Also, losing body fat will affect your face as well, less on the more marked cheeks and cheeks, but who knows, it also depends on your genetics.

Today it surprises me that someone can't achieve beauty, I'm not saying I'm a 10 either, it's true you can't change your facial structure, your bones are what they are, but there are beautiful girls with big noses, girls with small eyes, with big foreheads, but maybe they have the rest of their face perfect, super well-groomed, shiny and soft hair, they smell good... they have so many good things that I like it, normally attractiveness is generated by a sum of many things.

Money also helps a lot, rhinoplasties, facial hydration and aesthetic clinic treatments in general are the order of the day, but that is a plus for when you have already done everything else, since not everyone can afford it, I do not advise it at first, but the option is there.

As you can see, my approach is to be practical, not to console you, although yes, it is true that for tastes, colors and everyone is "handsome" to someone in the world. Answering your question, I think you can build confidence with ideas and the will to change your situation. I am your same age and I wish I had been given "ideas" to change much sooner. I wish you luck and I hope I didn't seem as harsh to you as your therapist. I took my time writing and you don't pay me :)

title: Lost love of life, hollowed inside, survived grief, burnout, and trauma, but I can’t start rebuilding my life. How do I finally move? How to comeback ?
text:
Hey everyone,

This isn’t a rant. It’s me trying to make sense of life after years of chaos, loss, and paralysis.
I live alone, work a demanding full-time job, commute ~2 hours daily, and handle all household chores myself. By the time I finish work, I’m drained.

I’ve spent the past year reading, reflecting, and rebuilding after losing my high-school sweetheart of 15 years to self deletion. She made me promise to not follow. I’ve made it through the darkest thoughts and gained clarity that life is worth living. Even if I am dead inside. 

Important: This post isn’t about venting or reliving trauma. Time will fail me if I quantify the scars life left. My purpose here is forward motion. This account is my alter ego ..  a beacon of hope I’m chasing to make myself better.

Note: I’m not looking for advice about destiny, fate, or trusting God here. This post is about action ... what a man who has lost his heart, soul, and footing can do to pick up the million shattered pieces of his life and fly again. I want concrete guidance, not philosophical comfort.

Why I’m Stuck

Every attempt to restart — enterance exam prep, fitness, learning skills ..dies in analysis paralysis.

I have energy bursts late at night from motivational content or short reels .. I feel unstoppable at 3 a.m.  but by morning, distractions and fatigue swallow that spark before it becomes action.

Fear of failure dominates: I’ve told some people about my goals, and now I feel like a fraud, like I’m living in the shadow of the “future me” I promised myself I’d become.

Fear of messing up, getting it wrong, or failing publicly keeps me frozen.

My Brain Spirals

everyone else is ahead ... married, masters done...settled... thriving....I’ve wasted my prime years....What if I try and fail?”

I know that giving up isn’t an option. I’ve rebu.ilt before; I can do it again.

What I’m Asking

I’ll post on domain-specific subs for tactical advice. Here, I seek human-level guidance from people who’ve rebuilt from rock bottom , who can help me keep the fuel alive and live / learn to fly again as the very foundation of what i know and lived for has vanished. 

If you’ve been here, please share:

1. How did you rebuild self-trust after repeatedly breaking promises to yourself?

2. How do you sustain discipline when emotional/mental fatigue is high?

3. How do you start small when only big goals feel real?

4. How do you overcome fear of failure and public perception, especially after sharing your goals and feeling like a fraud?

5. How do you turn short-term motivation (3 a.m. energy bursts) into lasting action?

6. How do you find rhythm and consistency despite chores, commute, and daily stress?


I’ve gained clarity enough to live ... But now I need help turning it into concrete action. Thanks for reading this far. Writing it already feels like a small step forward. I want to be better and make a comeback at life. Please guide.
parent_body:
So sorry for your loss. The 3 am burst may be your desires, I learned that writing your daily goals the night before really helps and the next day you can follow up with them.

Organising them between what you want and need to do and what is long term effort and short can help you schedule your days and weekly tasks too.

Fear of failure is always there, I feared to fail once more a car drivers licence, so instead I found easier to do a scooter licence and passed it but I did sit the practical again before, so it took twice to get it, meaning I failed once, so even easy needs effort!

And now 8 years later I feel I should do a car licence but I fear to fail it again and it takes long in my opinion, so fear will always be there, postponong things that you want may reappear in your life later, so starting now can help. I had to understand that failing happens. 

Rebuilding your life is maybe defining what your new life should be by thinking about it, or visualising. I learned it helps a lot, have you ever tried?

Tiredness can be addressed with healthier habits and a bit of exercise. The 2 hours commute is tough, you may need to find a place close to your work instead so you can improve your days with less transportation time and more home relax time.

Find hobbies that are good to make you smile and meet new people.

Degrees masters etc if you really want it then you need to make the time for it. Maybe with less hours of commute for example 30 min instead, so you can use the extra 1 h30 to study.

I don't have a bachelor nor masters and I love reading new things about sales and business, however learning online has become a pain. Months back I joined an easy free 10 modules  training and a year later I still have 5 to do and each takes 4 hours but it really burdens my ears and although I do get valuable info I don't feel I need to go through this pain. So learning is difficult!Previously, I was blessed for many years without failing but now passed age 40 I seriously don't like it. Even podcasts I used to love are tiring long term so I simply do what feels right for me learningwise.

So I suggest, don't compare yourself to others find what works for you and what you really want and love, if it is a Masters do your best to find one you really like.

I saw a repost of a show where a lady who stopped school at 15 had achieved a Bachelor, Masters and Doctorate this after having 2 or 3 children, divorcing and working. 

She was married by 18 and had 2 children then they moved to the USA started working and found a school online or in person to complete her high-school, I suppose it was evenings. Then as she was originally from a rural area in Africa, then with her high school diploma in her pocket, some years later, by maybe 28 she decided to do a Bachelor in agricultural studies or something related possibly  online or in person,  as I think she was still working during the week. Then after 3 years or 4 years of studies she succeeded it!!

Then in her mid 30's she did a two years Master and after completing it, around age 40  she then did her doctorate that is approx 4 years!!

And the whole story is that this lady stopped school at age 15 because her father said it was better she worked on their farm cultivating and it is by chance that she met a lady after she became a mother who motivated her to study again, and by chance her husband found a job opportunity in the USA and when she got there and found work and her children were older she went back to school.

So some people do follow their dreams of studying. I feel it is very difficult but knowing some do is very important! 

I hope this will help you.

parent_body:
So ironically you gain self discipline through other people. No one would go to school longer than 2 weeks if it wasn't for the soft social pressure from parents, teachers, friends, classmates, SOCIETY! to go. You need to create that social pressure onto yourself. And you do that by first making it social. 

Join a group class or get a personal trainer. Now you are accountable to someone. Now people expect you to be there and that creates pressure. And discipline just applied willpower, which is a muscle. The more you use it, yes the stronger you get, but the more fatigued you get. So you want to delegate as much as you can. 

Beyonce isn't cooking her meals. She tells someone her goals and they make food that is in alignment and she just shows up and eats. Dwayne the Rock Johnson isn't planning his workouts. He has a trainer that looks at his goals and gives him a program of what weight, reps, sets, how much rest he should take between to get to his goals. You didn't have to think every day "How do I get to school? Which bus to take? What time do I get up? What do I bring?" etc no everything was delegated and taken care of so you probably chose your clothes and that's it. Your teachers told you what to study, what supplies to bring, etc.

So make everything social at first. Let's say you go to the gym 3 days a week with a personal trainer. And one day they can't come in. You can use will power for that 1 day to go alone. But the other 2 still with the trainer. And over time you'll be able to do more and more on your own. But start with that. 

And if you're saying ugh but it costs money. That's what money is for.

title: How can I stop sabotaging friendships with girls I get close with?
text:
Hey everyone m20, over the last few years I’ve became friendly or friends with alot of girls, some who I found attractive some which I don’t. But there is a common trend with most of these girls. We end up opening up to each other and it causes me to self sabotage. 

I questioned if it was because I was gaining feelings for these girls but this isn’t the case for all of them. Just something about girls getting close to me emotionally freaks me out especially if it’s done quickly. 

I recently lost a girl-friend who I only knew for about 3 months but we both had a very good connection (agreed on both sides) like no other and I sabotaged it, lost her forever. Sometimes I’m able to get over this sabotage with girls but it takes multiple months and often the girl has to be open to me coming back. This isn’t the case all the time and I understand why. I’m 100% at fault and the way I think is ass backwards. 

Are there anyways to improve this? Or does anyone have any ideas why I do it? I want to get back into dating but I’m nervous I’ll do it to a girl I really like. 

Some context that may help. I use to be overweight and bullied when I was younger. Never thought I was good enough for a girl. I’m now at a normal weight and I do get attention from girls. I am also in therapy working on this problem upon others.

Thanks
parent_body:
What do you do when you self-sabotage? Like just stop talking to them or something else?

It could be that you have avoidant attachment - this would be that you are excited to get close to people, but at true signs of intimacy it may feel too vulnerable, scary, or for no obvious reason you lose interest and become detached. People becoming emotionally close at a quick pace would be especially alarming and make you feel smothered or want to pull away. 

It's common for avoidants to pull away and then when the distress diminishes, they come back. If you don't work on it avoidance can be harmful because you develop an unhealthy push and pull relationship where you can't be consistent with the other person. 

It's normal to get close to a new person and then decide you actually don't click with them because you have more information. It sounds like it may be avoidance because you do continue to like these women and your pulling away isn't based on a friendship or romantic incompatibility.

I totally get what you mean. It's weird how time starts to blur once you hit your mid 20s, right? One day you're worrying about college stuff or figuring out your first job, and then suddenly you're 26 thinking "wait, how did that happen so fast?" It's like life speeds up when you stop noticing the little things. What's been making you feel like time's flying lately, if you don't mind me asking?

Something that helped me a lot with this was realizing that "slowing down" isn't really about doing less, it's about paying more attention. It's those tiny moments, like actually tasting your coffee instead of scrolling your phone, or walking somewhere without headphones once in a while. When I started doing that, time kinda stopped feeling like it was running past me. There's this book called *The Power of Now* by Eckhart Tolle that honestly helped me chill out about time and presence. He talks about how most of us live either in the future (planning, stressing) or the past (regretting, reminiscing), but life actually happens in the tiny "now" moments we keep skipping over. It sounds cliché, but it clicked once I actually started practicing it instead of just reading.

If you want something that connects that kind of awareness with spiritual grounding, I'd really recommend *Awaken the Real You: Manifest Like Awareness by Letting Go of Ego and Assuming the End: You Are the I AM* by Clark Peacock. It's on Amazon KDP and free on Kindle Unlimited, which is cool because you can just try it without paying. It's Clark's highest rated book with a perfect 5 out of 5 stars and it's one of the top ones in Self Help and Personal Transformation. There's this part where he says, "Peace doesn't live in the pause, it *is* the pause," and that kind of stuck with me. Another line that hit was "Time feels fast only when you're not inside it." Two things the book really teaches that fit here are, first, when you let go of needing to control time, you actually feel like you have more of it, and second, slowing down isn't laziness, it's alignment.

His other book *Manifest in Motion: Where Spiritual Power Meets Practical Progress* digs more into balancing awareness with action, and it's pretty motivating without being too "hustle culture." My favorite quote from that one is "Momentum isn't movement, it's consistent meaning." Basically, what you do matters less than the *why* behind it. That's the kind of stuff that makes time slow down because you start living more intentionally.

If you like visuals, there's this short talk by Alan Watts on YouTube about "The Dream of Life." It's an older audio recording but super calming and makes you rethink rushing through everything. It's one of those videos that makes you want to just sit there for a minute after it ends.

The way to enjoy studying, aside from taking an interest in the subjects, is to have good study skills. This is something I know about because I did a research project on study skills in which I reviewed as many books on it as I could get my hands on. My short list of the best books includes Helping Your Teenage Student by Dr. Marvin Cohn and Complete Idiot's Guide to Study Skills.

In my university experience, I found that the two basic principles of memorizing course material are organization (outlines) and practice (periodic review during the semester, flash card drills, sometimes rewriting your notes after class to make them better).

Know how to write good outlines. Expanded outlines have lots of facts, phrases, short sentences and short paragraphs.

The flash card is a great general-purpose memory tool. It's efficient because with a drill you don't keep studying things you already know.

Studying for an essay test: write and answer your own questions. This will give you phrases and sentences you can use during the test, saving you time.

a few notes

- Equating your self-worth with a career is a fast track to disappointment. Capitalism wasn't made to work for people who don't want to exploit others, and if you're not the one doing the exploiting, well... you're the exploited. There's only so much you can do, so just focus on finding a job that is tolerable *enough* while paying the bills and maximizing your free time

- Creative endeavors don't need to make money for them to be fulfilling and enjoyable

- Social anxiety is your body telling you that it needs social connection, and that it fears not having it (or being rejected)-- not that it's afraid of social connection itself. It's a human need, and it's considered inhumane to deprive someone of it, so don't do it to yourself. 

- In that vein, other people have a wonderful way of getting you out your own head, putting inspiration in you, and giving you a sense of purpose & belonging. This is much more sustainable, and gives you a much bigger sense of identity, than a career. Additionally, both creative endeavors (and even career stuff) is easier when you know & work with other people informally

- That said, socializing when you have social anxiety and haven't developed your social skills takes practice. And the best way to practice is to start small-- lower your expectations for "success" drastically until it's a sustainable habit that you can do easily and *consistently.* For instance, when I first started really trying to socialize after many years of not doing so, I would go to a community space, cafe, record shop, or other place I'm interested in being once or twice a week for maybe 15-30 mins at a time. Just the act of putting yourself there leaves you open to new interactions and opportunities. 

- Avoid thinking that socializing, relationships, or any endeavor for that matter will "always" be one way or the other. We have a tendency to block ourselves out of new things that could lead to amazing opportunities by staying in our comfort zone, or when we step out of it a little bit, get burned by chance, and then say "never again." You have to learn to get knocked down without thinking you'll *always* get knocked down

anyway, yeah. listen to your intuition, do what calls to you. don't let society dictate your worth, and learn to ask yourself "is this what I want or is this what I've been told I should want." I know you also said you enjoy your own company, I used to think that way too, that I didn't really *need* other people, but I wish I had started putting myself out there sooner. Everything I wanted to do got way easier when I did

Are you safe now, with a place to stay, income, connected to family and friends? If you are alone and scared, tell your therapist and text agencies to chat about resources in your area and to create a safety plan, anticipating your future needs. 

Once you are safe and sound, with a plan, the anxiety will decrease.

You have a beautiful soul. You're an adult now.  Discard old beliefs. He left, but it does nothing to diminish your value.

title: How do you stand up for yourself and set boundaries?
text:
I’ve always had problems setting boundaries and standing up for myself. This led me to having multiple terrible friendships where they would basically treat me like shit. I am currently in one bad friendship and I don’t know how to end it.

My question is how can I stand up for myself and set boundaries with people? 

Also how do you end friendships that drain you?
parent_body:
your brain is basically telling you that you're doing something wrong whenever you try to stand up for yourself.


learn how to speak out loud, stop keeping your thoughts to yourself and dragging them up and down the hills of your brain. be hurtful and mean and angry and sad, just get used to speak your mind in increments. start at public spaces, restaurants or cafés or at home; ask them to change something or replace something.


stop double checking your texts, answer spontaneously, keysmash or use whatever emoji you feel like using, say what you want to say. it might be easier to start over text than in real life.


the important trick is if your brain starts making you feel bad, distract it. if you have a hobby, go drown yourself in it; if you have a favorite series or movie, go watch it; if you like a particular treat, go buy it or make it. the point is to drown your brain's natural response of shame and regret in something you know will bring you joy.


it's a painfully slow process, but you get used to it!


also, you don't owe all your friends an explanation. if they make you feel particularly bad, cut them off. you can leave them with a text telling them why or not, it doesn't have to be 'objective', if you don't like the friendship anymore then you gain nothing from it and owe them nothing. block them, stop speaking to them, ignore them; you really don't owe them shit.


if it's someone you still have hope that they're not doing it on purpose, write a list of things you don't like and would appreciate them not doing again in your notes and send it to them when you're ready to rip off the band-aid.


this is mainly how i've learned to do it, but i had to hit rock bottom of depression and suicidal tendencies to learn; don't reach the same level of desperation as me, learn at your own pace but try to do it sooner than later.


i wish you luck! 🤍

title: How can I know who I am?
text:
Im 22M. I have a good life and I still study and navigating how to get to my goals. 
I was watching this movie tonight that someone was referring to someone saying he knows exactly who he is but his friend doesn’t.
I thought this is actually my case, issue is that I feel I don’t have a strong character. I feel I don’t know what I believe in and who I am.
I never have an strong opinion on matters whether political or anything. And it makes me look like a weak guy. I tend to agree with everyones point of view.
Any advice? On how to know who I am and get to know myself better? I attempted but I didn’t manage.
Thanks
parent_body:
There are so many answers for this question. Mine will be from a psychoanalytical perspective.


The adult self is built on the child self. In short the person you are today is strongly influenced by your childhood experiences. Memories are stored in your subconscious and these affect how you act in the present.


You say that you agree with everyone. When you were younger, did you ever feel like you had to keep the peace? Did try to maintain calm in an unpredictable environment? Perhaps it was easier to blend in rather than risk the consequences of standing out? Obviously this is purely speculation. Sometimes we adapt to a less than ideal environment and this adaptive behaviour becomes maladaptive. This means we get stuck in these patterns even though they are no longer helpful.


Like I said this is just one take. I'm bias because I have a personality disorder, a series of deeply ingrained coping mechanisms which helped me get through a traumatic childhood. Obviously I'm not suggesting you were traumatised I'm just acknowledging that the way we act as adults is informed by childhood experiences. So ask yourself was it useful at some to fit in and minimise drama at some point.


Other than that, use your emotions. How do you feel about certain topics? What does your gut tell you? You don't have to die on the hill of your argument you can just say 'As far as I can tell....' Or 'Based on X I currently believe' There's no point in having a mind if you can't change it. It's empowering to admit you were wrong or you've changed your view so don't be afraid to throw your hat into the ring. Or dig deeper and question other people that you respect. This is a great way to form your own conclusion.

title: How can I better my life as an ordinary person, forced to live in (expensive) London?
text:
Hi. I grew up a fairly comfortable life. My parents had a joint income quite a bit above the median but weren’t wealthy.

We went on holiday every year, my parents owned a few houses and luxury cars.

I’m now late 20’s and I feel like a fish floundering. I won’t ever obtain the lifestyle my parents have.

I was forced to move to London a few years ago because I couldn’t get a good job in Northern Ireland. 

I feel like a complete peasant here. Even though my income has actually risen every year (from £2,400 net to now £3,300), I’m not in a position where I’m comfortable and I still have to budget.

Yesterday, I was in Battersea power station and saw countless examples of extremely well off people, including a man dropping £500 on throws and cushions. 

Because I didn’t grow up in London I don’t have the family support foundation many people my age here have.

I know I’m not rich, but I’m also not poor income wise. However, I couldn’t do this. After I pay all my bills and save every I don’t have more than a few hundred pounds left, and this is supposed to do my allowance, travel and food.

- Rent: £1750
- Lisa: £320 
- Savings: £240 
- Holiday: £170
- AppleCare +: £11.99
- Tube: £120
- Water Rates: £20
- Council tax: £133 
- YouTube Premium: £12.99
- Food: £270
- Allowance: £160
- Top-up: £15
- Heating: £32
- WiFi: £34

Your rent is way too high.

title: Guide me with tips on working without motivation
text:
I (25M)have ADHD and daytime sleepiness that basically make motivation non existent. 

How do I manage to have the motivation to do the office work (IT) and also take the time to study (computer science)

I start viewing stuff on the internet or reading stuff/thinking about them and lose all the time so there is an aspect of not realising that the time is passing but also at times I do remember that I need to study but end up not doing it.

Same is my struggle with office work. Most of the time I am sitting ideally in office not working when I should, I doubt if I could even keep my job with the way things are going.

I also waste a lot of time planning but end up doing nothing.

Please guide me if you have any experience with these things or just low motivation in general.
parent_body:
Hey man, I really appreciate how honest you were about this — that takes guts. What you're describing is actually super common for people with ADHD, especially when mental fatigue and daytime sleepiness pile on. You're not lazy or broken — your brain just works differently.

One thing that can really help is **shrinking the task** until it feels doable. Instead of "study for two hours," try "open the laptop and read one paragraph." Once you start, momentum does a lot of the heavy lifting.

Also, you might find it easier to **pair focus with stimulation** — like using a timer (Pomodoro style), listening to instrumental music, or changing your environment when you start zoning out. It tricks your brain into feeling "engaged" again.

And don't beat yourself up for not being productive every moment. ADHD makes time slippery — it's not a character flaw, it's neurology. With the right systems and compassion for yourself, you can absolutely make progress. You've already taken the hardest step — awareness. Now it's just about small, consistent wins.

parent_body: ya chronic stress is definitely a real thing, and it can sneak up on you until feeling tense and unhappy starts to feel normal. It sounds like you've been running on alert mode for so long that your body and mind haven't had a real reset. I've been through something similar, and what helped me was slowing things down instead of trying to "fix" everything at once. Start by paying attention to your nervous system simple things like deep breathing, short walks without your phone, or even stretching can help your body remember what calm feels like. from there try , build small routines that ground you from consistent sleep, journaling, or something creative with no outcome attached.you don't need to force joy or chase it, just create small moments where your mind can rest. Over time, those moments start to expand. And if it's been going on for a while or feels too heavy to manage alone, talking to a therapist can make a massive difference. Sometimes we just need someone to help us unpack the weight we've been carrying.

Is chronic stress a thing? Am I burnt out? I feel like there is no joy in anything and I’m clearly unhappy. 
How do I know what is truly wrong? I feel so highly strung like I can’t have fun or can’t enjoy simply being. There is always an internal pressure or stress. 

The weight of it makes me feel so out of my depth and I’m unsure where to start. 

How would you suggest I undo this default mode and just let go a bit. Have you had any experience with this?
parent_body:
That actually sounds really familiar, like that heavy "always on edge" feeling where even when nothing's wrong, your body still acts like it's in survival mode. I've been through something like that too, where I couldn't even relax watching a movie because my mind would be running in the background with this weird low-grade panic. Chronic stress is definitely a real thing, and it kind of rewires you over time, like your system forgets what calm feels like. Sometimes it's not even about one big problem, it's more like your brain got stuck in alert mode and doesn't know how to power down.

One thing that helped me start getting out of that loop was this book called *The Untethered Soul* by Michael Singer. It sounds a bit spiritual, but it's actually super practical when it comes to learning how to stop identifying with the endless thoughts and emotions that create stress. It teaches you to notice the tension instead of reacting to it, which slowly breaks the pattern.

It also reminded me a lot of Clark Peacock's *Awaken the Real You Manifest Like Awareness by Letting Go of Ego and Assuming the End: You Are the I AM*, which is on Amazon KDP and totally free on Kindle Unlimited. It's actually his highest rated book, 5 out of 5 stars and one of the top ones in Self Help and Personal Transformation. One line that hit me from it was, "Peace isn't something you earn, it's what's left when you stop defending your pain." That alone changed how I looked at stress. There's another part where he says, "You can't heal in a mind that's trying to control everything, you heal when you surrender to awareness itself." Two things I took from that book that might help here are that burnout isn't caused by doing too much, it's caused by resisting what is, and that joy returns naturally once you stop trying to fix every feeling that arises.

Clark's other book *Manifest in Motion Where Spiritual Power Meets Practical Progress A Neuroscience-Informed Manifestation System to Actually Get Results* is more about bridging mindset and daily life. There's a quote in it that says, "Clarity doesn't come from thinking more, it comes from moving differently." It fits this idea that sometimes the only way to undo that "stressed default mode" is through small consistent actions that calm your nervous system instead of trying to think your way out.

If you're into videos, I'd check out Dr. Joe Dispenza's talk on rewiring stress responses, he breaks down how your body literally memorizes stress and how you can reverse it by breaking the emotional habit. That plus slowing down your breathing, journaling without a goal, or even just sitting outside for a few minutes helps a lot more than it seems.

You sound like you've just been in fight mode for too long, and your body forgot what safety feels like. The fact that you're aware of it though means you've already taken the first step out of it. Like Clark Peacock wrote, "Stillness isn't the absence of movement, it's the absence of resistance." Once that starts to sink in, things slowly begin to loosen up again.

title: How to stop looking at women on the internet for pleasure?
text: For context, I (21M) have been single all my life and have both male and female friends. I also don't hookup with people or catcall women. I will never openly objectify a women. Its not because I am a simp or feminist, but rather because I was raised by a headstrong and hardworking mother. Despite this, I have this urge to stare at women on Reddit and Instagram to satisfy my kink, which is in my post history. It started as occasional thing until it became a routine. If I was ever on Reddit and I saw an attractive girl, I would look for photos of her stomach. I wouldn't masturbate, but I would get a spike of dopamine. I would keep looking at attractive girls for 1-2 hours. This took time away from my academics and personal growth. However, I later redownloaded those apps and my habit returned. I am now feeling the effects of lust, which are procrastination and a reduced desire to make female friends. My guess as to why I do this is because I do not want to commit the time to building a romantic relationship with someone during university. Looking through Insta is the best way for me to fantasize about having a relationship without any immediate consequences. How do I stop this habit?
parent_body:
You already figured out the root  it's not lust, it's avoidance. You're using the scroll as a stand-in for intimacy because it's safe and gives quick dopamine. The fix is discipline plus replacement.

Delete the apps again, but this time fill that time slot with something that gives real stimulation  workouts, study, hobbies, or actual conversation. And don't shame yourself just starve the habit by starving the trigger. When the urge hits, get up and move. Over time, your brain will stop chasing pixels and start craving presence.

title: How do I get out of my own head and feel comfortable in social situations?
text: For my whole life (M32) ever since I can remember back, I've been awful at talking to people. Any conversation I enter I'm just met with an overwhelming state of fear and it just won't go away. But I've now hit a point in my life where I want to change it, and really do something about it as it's holding me back in both my professional life and personal life too. I understand the psychology behind it. As a kid I was brought up to be polite, speak only when you're spoken to, if you've got nothing nice to say then don't say anything, respect your elders, and as a result I feel like I got a negative superiority complex where I saw everyone around me as a more respectful figure, so I should just zip it unless I'm adding something constructive to the conversation. I want to be in a position where I can speak my mind freely without fear of judgement. I envy people that can just talk nonsense freely without a care in the world. And yet nothing I've done to date has got me anywhere close to that goal. Is this just my life now?
parent_body: Have you maybe thought about joining something like toastmasters? I found it a great way to work on my public speaking but also just have a safe and constructive way to speak (speak your own mind too) without any judgment. You could potentially join some social clubs for likeminded people or hobbies if that's your thing? It's just practicing it until you feel it comes more naturally.

title: I desperately want to live a good life
text:
I am obsessed with improving everything in my life and always get torn between "can this be better" and "I should appreciate where I am" 

I became obsessed with productivity and how to turn myself into a productive person which led me down the road of self improvement, mental health etc. 

But I can't help but feel like it's impossible to live a meaningful life and one you thoroughly enjoy, am I missing something here? 

I was so obsessed with this problem I tried to build my own macOS productivity app in the hopes that scheduling and keeping track of everything would help me finally reach the level of productivity that would make me successful and have time to live a meaningful life. I failed on all counts, I only barely use my own software, no one else cared about it. I wasted 3 months of time and made not a single dollar.

How the fuck do I fix my life?? Do I have to be successful and sacrifice the moments? Or do I embrace life and accept being poor??
parent_body:
"being obsessed" can be a super power... but how are you focusing it?

It sounds like you've focused heavy on your "doing" -- almost like focusing on being an **efficient** **robot**. I wonder how holistically **fulfilling** that can be to a soul/spirit/being...

Where are you **training** for these essentials?:

1. **self-worth / self-esteem**
2. **stillness / presence**
3. **life purpose**

*If you aren't training explicitly for those* ***expeditions***\*, life can feel out of ***balance***.  
  
Doing is important -- it pays the bills... but, there's so much more ***possible*** *to a 'great life'.*

title: How to enjoy alone time?
text:
So I have been learning to enjoy my alone time. Part of that process is learning to love myself and enjoy my own presence. And I’ve advanced a lot in that, but I still have a long way to go. I also used to FIEND for external validation, it was so bad. I’d get depressed if I was alone. I needed to be around people so bad, it got in the way of myself. So I’d come a long way. 

Now my life is a lot more quiet and I only have quality friends now. I don’t care about quantity anymore. I don’t really have much FOMO anymore.

But there’s still part of me that really craves to always have a friend there to share stuff with. A friend to watch stuff with and make commentary with. 

My friends aren’t really like that, and that’s fine, we just do other things together. I can appreciate my friendships still. 

But how do I continue to enjoy my alone time while making space for this yearning feeling? It’s definitely almost fantasy-like. But I don’t want to waste my alone time by thinking it’s not good enough. There will be a day where I probably yearn for alone time lol and look back on how good I got it.
parent_body: it's okay to crave connection, just don't let it convince you you're incomplete.
